title: AI finds security bugs faster than they get fixed. Should the 90day rule change?
content:
AI is finding security bugs faster than maintainers can fix them. Should the 90-day disclosure deadline change?
Jump to a position (4)
What this question is about
When security researchers find a vulnerability, they usually tell the project privately and publish the details 90 days later, or sooner once a fix is out. Google's Project Zero made this deadline the common standard. It exists to push vendors to fix bugs instead of sitting on them.
In 2026 AI models began finding bugs at a scale nobody planned for. Published CVEs roughly doubled in a year, PostgreSQL delayed its release to keep up with fixes, and many reports land on projects run by volunteers. The same tools can also help attackers. The question is whether 90 days still protects users, and if not, which way the deadline should move.
Positions
4 positions, in no order of merit. Open one for its full case.
Researchers keep giving projects 90 days to fix a reported bug before details are published, as Project Zero and most of the industry do today.
3 reasons4 sources3 objections from other positions
- A fixed deadline is what makes vendors fix bugs at all; before it, reported flaws could sit unpatched for years. Strongest objection (Leaves something out), for Give maintainers more time: Volunteer projects like FFmpeg aren’t vendors stalling; they simply don’t have the people to fix a flood of reports in any deadline.
Read the full case (3 reasons)
Projects, especially volunteer ones, get longer or flexible deadlines, and finders slow the pace of their reports to what a project can handle.
2 reasons5 sources2 objections from other positions
- Maintainers can’t keep up: PostgreSQL delayed its whole release because fixing AI-found bugs swallowed its reviewers’ time. Strongest objection (Leaves something out), for Shorten the deadline: Attackers won’t slow down to match a project’s capacity, so a longer embargo mainly keeps users in the dark.
Read the full case (2 reasons)
The deadline stays, but companies that report bugs at scale with AI also have to supply tested patches or pay for the work of fixing them.
3 reasons3 sources2 objections from other positions
- Finding bugs has far outrun fixing them, so the bottleneck is the fixing, not the deadline. Strongest objection (Leaves something out): Several AI companies are already paying: seven of them gave $12.5 million through the Linux Foundation for triage and fixes.
Read the full case (3 reasons)
Disclosure deadlines get shorter, so users learn about flaws sooner, even if some are published before a fix exists.
2 reasons2 sources4 objections from other positions
- Attackers have the same AI tools, so a bug one company finds is likely to be found by someone else long before 90 days pass. Strongest objection (Overstated), for Keep 90 days: No attacks on CVE-2026-98432 had been reported even after its exploit was announced, so real attackers are still slower than the theory.
Read the full case (2 reasons)

report.summary: AI is flooding open-source projects with vulnerability reports, sparking debate over whether the 90-day disclosure deadline should stretch, shrink, or shift fix-work to the AI companies finding the bugs.
report.background: For years, the norm in vulnerability disclosure has been coordinated disclosure: a researcher tells a project privately, and details go public 90 days later — or sooner once a patch ships. Google's Project Zero popularised that deadline, and most of the industry followed. The rationale is simple: without a clock, vendors can sit on reported flaws indefinitely. In 2026 that system met a scale it was never designed for. AI models began finding bugs in volumes nobody planned for — published CVEs roughly doubled in a year, PostgreSQL delayed its whole release because AI-found bugs swamped its human reviewers, and many reports land on projects run by unpaid volunteers like FFmpeg, which has dismissed some AI submissions as 'CVE slop'. The same tooling is available to attackers, so the debate is not whether disclosure matters, but what pace and shape it should take.
key_points: The 90-day rule exists to force action: a fixed public deadline is what stops vendors from parking reported flaws indefinitely. Before it became standard, bugs could sit unpatched for years. Critics of changing it warn that any weakening removes the only real pressure on slow vendors — and that everyone already knows the 90-day norm, so rewriting it now would create confusion just as report volume peaks.

The bottleneck moved from finding to fixing: AI can surface bugs in minutes, but patching still takes human reviewers. PostgreSQL 19 slipped to November 19 because AI-found reports consumed maintainer time, and volunteer projects argue they are not stalling vendors — they simply lack people to absorb a flood of low-quality reports.

Four positions are on the table: keep 90 days as-is; give projects longer or flexible deadlines and let finders throttle their reporting rate; keep the deadline but require AI-scale finders to supply tested patches or fund the fix work; or shorten deadlines so users learn about flaws sooner, on the argument that attackers with the same tools will find the bug anyway.

Money is starting to move: seven AI companies contributed $12.5 million through the Linux Foundation for triage and remediation, which supporters of the 'finder pays' position cite as proof the model works. That reframes disclosure as a cost-allocation problem, not just a calendar problem.

The attacker-speed argument is contested: shortening deadlines assumes adversaries will rediscover bugs quickly, but one cited case — CVE-2026-98432 — saw no reported attacks even after a public exploit announcement, suggesting real-world exploitation still lags the theory.
report.impact: For the AI industry, disclosure policy is becoming a governance and liability question: companies that can find bugs at scale may soon be expected to fund or perform the fixes, turning security research into a paid obligation rather than a public good. For developers and maintainers, the near-term reality is triage overload — more reports, more of them low quality, and pressure to adopt automated patch pipelines and severity filtering. For regular users, the trade-off is visible: a longer embargo keeps people exposed to known-but-unpatched flaws, while a shorter one pushes advisories out before fixes exist, feeding update fatigue and, in the worst case, giving attackers a head start they can exploit against stragglers.
report.tools: To follow along or get involved: the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) and the Linux Foundation's security fund for triage and remediation; GitHub Security Advisories and Dependabot / Renovate for patch flow; Google's OSS-Fuzz and its Big Sleep AI bug-finder; CodeQL and Semgrep for static analysis; CVE.org and NVD for tracking the volume surge; and the oss-security mailing list for disclosure norms in practice.
